fields.title: Recording outside police station — phone seized
fields.story_text:
On March 15, 2024, around 2:30 in the afternoon, I was standing on the public sidewalk directly in front of the Springfield Police Department at 400 Main Street, Springfield, Illinois. I was recording the exterior of the building and the officers coming and going, which I have done before and understand to be legal on a public sidewalk.

After about ten minutes, Officer David Ruiz, badge number 1142, came out the front door and walked directly toward me. He told me I was not allowed to record the police station and that I needed to leave. I told him I was on a public sidewalk and had every right to be there and to record. He said I was loitering and that if I didn't put the camera away he would arrest me.

I continued recording and told him again I was exercising my First Amendment rights. At that point he grabbed my phone out of my hand without warning, turned it off, and placed it in his pocket. He then grabbed my left arm and placed me in handcuffs. A second officer, Sergeant Linda Torres, badge number 887, came outside and watched without intervening. Officer Ruiz told me I was being detained for disorderly conduct.

I was held on the sidewalk in handcuffs for approximately 35 minutes. No citation was issued. My phone was eventually returned, but the recording had been deleted. I never consented to the deletion and I never gave them permission to access my phone. I was then told to leave or I would be arrested. I left.

I have video from a second phone I was carrying in my back pocket that captured most of the encounter. The second recording shows Officer Ruiz taking my primary phone and shows Sergeant Torres watching the entire event.

As a result of this I experienced significant emotional distress, missed a work shift because I was detained so long, and lost the original recording which I had intended to post publicly. I want to file a complaint for First Amendment retaliation, unlawful seizure of my property, and the department's apparent policy of preventing recording outside the station.

fields.title: Recording at public library — escorted out, threatened with arrest
fields.story_text:
On July 8, 2024, at approximately 11:00 AM, I entered the Riverside County Public Library at 200 Civic Center Drive in Riverside, California. The library is a public building funded by taxpayer money and open to the public. I had my phone out and was recording the interior common areas — the lobby, the front desk, and the public reading room — as part of my practice of auditing public facilities.

Within about five minutes a library employee, who later identified herself as the branch manager, Maria Castillo, approached me and told me recording was not allowed inside the library. I asked her to show me the policy and she said she didn't have to show me anything and that I needed to stop immediately. I asked if there was a posted rule and she said the library had a no-recording policy.

I continued recording and told her I believed recording in a public building open to the public was protected by the First Amendment. She walked away and approximately four minutes later two officers from the Riverside Police Department arrived — Officer James Polk, badge 3341, and Officer Wayne Briggs, badge 3489. Officer Polk told me I was trespassing and that I needed to leave the building immediately or I would be arrested. I asked what law I was violating. He said I was violating the library's rules and that was sufficient.

I was escorted out of the building by both officers. No arrest was made and no citation was issued, but Officer Polk told me if I returned with a camera I would be arrested for trespassing. He also told me the next time I came in he would be watching for me.

A bystander who was seated at a reading table, a man named Carl Webb, witnessed the entire encounter and told me afterward he thought what the officers did was wrong. He gave me his phone number.

I suffered emotional distress from being publicly escorted out. I want to pursue a claim for First Amendment retaliation and viewpoint-based exclusion from a public building.

fields.title: Recording at city hall — detained in lobby, ID demanded
fields.story_text:
On September 3, 2024, around 9:45 in the morning, I entered the lobby of City Hall at 1 Government Plaza in Columbus, Ohio. I was carrying my phone and recording openly. The lobby is a public area open to all citizens during business hours. There are no posted signs prohibiting recording.

A security guard named Robert Haynes, employed by the City of Columbus, approached me almost immediately and told me I was not permitted to record in City Hall. I asked him to point me to the rule. He said it was city policy. I asked him to show me the written policy. He refused and instead called for backup on his radio.

Within a few minutes a second security guard arrived along with Detective Carol Simmons of the Columbus Police Department, badge 5512, who was apparently stationed inside the building. Detective Simmons told me I needed to identify myself or I would be arrested for obstruction. I asked what I was obstructing. She said I was obstructing the security staff. I told her I was standing still in a public lobby doing nothing other than recording.

I was then told to stand against the wall. I complied. Detective Simmons took my name and date of birth. She ran my information — I could see her on her radio — and after about 20 minutes told me I was free to go but that if I came back with a recording device I would be banned from the building.

At no point was I advised of any specific law I had broken. No citation was issued. The entire encounter was recorded on my phone, which I had kept running in my jacket pocket after they first approached me, and also by the City Hall security cameras which I believe captured the full interaction.

I am seeking to file a complaint for unlawful detention, compelled identification without reasonable suspicion, and First Amendment retaliation.

fields.title: Recording traffic stop from public sidewalk — arrested for obstruction
fields.story_text:
On November 19, 2024, at around 8:15 PM, I was walking on the public sidewalk on Oak Avenue in Memphis, Tennessee, when I observed a Memphis Police Department traffic stop taking place on the street. Two officers had pulled over a vehicle and one driver was being asked to step out. I stopped on the sidewalk approximately 30 feet away and began recording with my phone. I was not in the roadway. I was not speaking to the officers or the driver. I was standing still on the sidewalk.

One of the officers, Officer Sean McGrath, badge 2278, noticed me recording and walked over to me. He told me to put the phone away. I told him I was on a public sidewalk and had a right to record. He told me I was interfering with a police investigation. I told him I was 30 feet away and had said nothing. He grabbed my phone from my hand and told me to put my hands behind my back. I asked if I was being arrested. He said yes, for obstruction of justice.

I was handcuffed and placed in the back of a police cruiser. The second officer, Officer Patricia Nguyen, badge 2301, stayed with the traffic stop. I was transported to the Shelby County jail and booked. I was held for approximately six hours before being released on my own recognizance. The obstruction charge was later dismissed by the prosecutor.

My phone was held as evidence for three weeks. When it was returned the video had been cleared. I had a cloud backup that captured most of the encounter before my phone was taken.

I lost wages from missing two days of work. I was publicly humiliated during the arrest on a busy street. I have significant anxiety since the arrest. I want to file for First Amendment retaliation, unlawful arrest without probable cause, and destruction of evidence.

fields.title: Recording at DMV — removed and phone smashed
fields.story_text:
On February 6, 2024, at approximately 1:00 PM, I entered the Department of Motor Vehicles office at 500 State Road in Aurora, Colorado. I was openly recording with my phone. The DMV is a public government office. I had researched this beforehand and found no Colorado law prohibiting recording in public government buildings.

Almost immediately a DMV supervisor, who identified herself as Patricia Dunn, told me to stop recording. I asked for the legal basis. She said it was DMV policy to protect customer privacy. I pointed out I was recording the government employees at the counter, not other customers. She became agitated and called Aurora Police.

Officer Timothy Walsh, badge 6643, arrived within about eight minutes. He told me I needed to leave the building. I asked if I was being trespassed. He said yes, the DMV was asking me to leave. I said I would leave but asked for his name and badge number. He refused to give me his badge number and when I raised my phone to capture his badge visually he grabbed my wrist, twisted it, and knocked my phone to the floor. The phone's screen shattered on impact.

I was escorted out of the building. My wrist was sore and bruised for several days. I went to an urgent care clinic two days later and was told I had a soft tissue sprain. I have the medical records.

A woman in line behind me, Angela Reyes, witnessed Officer Walsh grab my wrist and knock my phone down. She was upset and also left the DMV shortly after. I have her contact information.

I am seeking a complaint for excessive force, unlawful seizure of my person, First Amendment retaliation, and destruction of my personal property. The phone cost $800 to replace.

fields.title: Recording police outside courthouse — detained and searched
fields.story_text:
On April 22, 2024, around 10:30 AM, I was standing on the public plaza in front of the Hamilton County Courthouse in Cincinnati, Ohio. I was recording the exterior of the building and the officers posted outside at the security entrance. I was not inside the building. I was on the open public plaza which is accessible to anyone.

A Hamilton County Sheriff's deputy, Deputy Frank Olson, badge S-441, approached me and told me I could not record the courthouse entrance. I told him I was on a public plaza and not inside the courthouse. He said it was a security zone and recording was not permitted. I continued recording and told him I disagreed.

He radioed for backup and two more deputies arrived, Deputy Rosa Martinez, badge S-517, and Deputy Ken Atwood, badge S-388. Deputy Atwood told me to put my hands on the wall. I asked if I was being detained. He said yes. I asked why. He said for suspicious activity and possibly for violating courthouse security protocol.

I was patted down. They found nothing. My phone was taken and held for the duration of the detention — approximately 45 minutes. They eventually returned my phone and told me I was free to go but that if I came back and recorded I would be arrested for criminal trespassing.

The recording was still intact when my phone was returned. I also had a second camera — a small body camera clipped to my shirt — that recorded the entire detention including the pat-down.

I want to file a complaint for unlawful detention, unlawful search, seizure of my phone without a warrant, and First Amendment retaliation for recording government officials in a public space.

fields.title: Recording police station lobby — cited for loitering, recording deleted
fields.story_text:
On June 10, 2024, at around 3:00 PM, I entered the lobby of the Tucson Police Department's east substation at 9310 East Golf Links Road in Tucson, Arizona. The lobby is open to the public during business hours. I walked in and began recording — I was filming the lobby area, the front desk, and the officers visible behind the counter.

The desk officer, Officer Michelle Grant, badge 4421, immediately told me I was not allowed to record inside the police station. I told her that a police station lobby open to the public is a public space. She told me I needed to stop or she would call her supervisor.

Her supervisor, Sergeant Paul Vega, badge 3102, came out from the back and told me to hand him my phone. I refused and asked for the legal authority. He said I was creating a disturbance. I pointed out I had not spoken loudly or done anything disruptive. He said he was issuing me a citation for loitering and that I needed to leave.

He wrote me a loitering citation and then told me I had to surrender my phone before leaving as it was evidence. I told him I did not consent to surrendering my phone. He and a second officer, Officer Derek Lane, badge 4509, physically took my phone from my hand. After about 20 minutes my phone was returned. The recording had been deleted. I was told to leave or I would be arrested.

The loitering citation was later dismissed in court.

I am seeking relief for First Amendment retaliation, unlawful seizure of my phone, deletion of my recording without consent or a warrant, and malicious prosecution based on the baseless loitering citation.

fields.title: Recording city council meeting — ejected during public session
fields.story_text:
On August 14, 2024, at 6:00 PM, I attended a regularly scheduled public meeting of the Bayside City Council at City Hall, 100 Harbor Boulevard, Bayside, Florida. The meeting is open to the public under Florida's Sunshine Law. I was seated in the public gallery and recording the meeting with my phone on a small tripod, pointed at the council dais.

Approximately 25 minutes into the meeting, Council Chair Beverly Stanton instructed a city security officer, Officer Marcus Webb of the Bayside Police Department, badge 771, to approach me. Officer Webb told me I needed to put away my camera. I asked if there was a rule against recording public meetings. He said the council had a policy against recording devices in the chamber.

I told him that Florida law guarantees the right to record public meetings of government bodies. He said he was not a lawyer and I needed to comply or leave. I stated for the record that I was invoking my right to record a public government meeting. Council Chair Stanton then ordered me removed from the chamber.

Officer Webb and another officer, Officer Dana Chen, badge 802, physically escorted me out of the chamber and into the hallway. My recording device and tripod were taken at the door and held for approximately one hour before being returned. I was told I was banned from attending future council meetings while recording.

Another attendee, James Tran, recorded my removal on his phone from the gallery. He has agreed to provide his recording.

I am seeking relief for First Amendment violations including retaliation for recording a public meeting, viewpoint-based ejection from a public forum, and the city's unconstitutional no-recording policy applied to public government meetings.

fields.title: Recording on public sidewalk near protest — arrested, phone confiscated overnight
fields.story_text:
On October 5, 2024, at approximately 4:45 PM, I was standing on the public sidewalk on Jefferson Avenue in Detroit, Michigan, near a permitted protest that was taking place. I was not part of the protest. I was documenting events as an independent citizen journalist. I was on the public sidewalk, not blocking foot traffic, and not interacting with protesters or counter-protesters.

A Detroit Police Department officer, Officer Bryan Kowalski, badge 7734, approached me and told me to move. I asked if I was in a restricted area. He said the entire block was restricted. I asked to see the order or permit establishing the restriction. He said he didn't need to show me anything. I stayed on the sidewalk, continuing to record, and asked if I was being detained.

Officer Kowalski told me I was under arrest for failure to comply with a lawful order. I was handcuffed. A second officer, Officer Tamara Jackson, badge 7891, took my phone and placed it in a property bag. I was transported to the Detroit Detention Center and held overnight — approximately 14 hours — before being released. The charge was failure to obey a police order. That charge was dismissed three weeks later.

My phone was not returned to me upon release. I had to make three separate trips to the property room over two weeks before it was returned. The recording on the phone remained intact.

I had to take two days off from my job as a delivery driver, costing me approximately $340 in lost wages. I also paid $500 for a bail bondsman. I experienced significant anxiety and sleep disruption in the weeks following the arrest.

I want to file a complaint for unlawful arrest, First Amendment retaliation, prolonged property seizure without probable cause, and the department's pattern of arresting journalists and citizen auditors at public events.

fields.title: Recording at public park — officer demands ID, detains for 40 minutes
fields.story_text:
On January 27, 2024, at around 2:00 in the afternoon, I was in Elmwood Park, a public city park at 800 Park Drive in Kansas City, Missouri. I was walking through the park recording the grounds, the pavilion, and a group of city workers doing maintenance. I was not interfering with anyone and was on a public footpath.

Officer Christine Malone, badge 5581, of the Kansas City Police Department approached me and asked what I was doing. I told her I was recording in a public park. She asked for my ID. I asked if I was being detained and what the basis for detention was. She said she was investigating suspicious activity. I asked what specifically was suspicious. She said someone had called in a complaint about a person recording in the park.

I asked again if I was free to go. She said no, I was being detained pending her investigation. She called for a second officer, Officer Gary Pham, badge 5740, who arrived approximately ten minutes later. Officer Pham told me that parks in Kansas City required a permit for commercial filming. I told him I was not filming commercially, I was a citizen exercising my First Amendment rights. He said he would have to verify that.

I was held on the footpath, both officers present, for approximately 40 minutes total. No permit was ever mentioned in writing. No citation was issued. My ID was taken, run through dispatch, and returned with no findings. I was eventually told I was free to go.

The full 40-minute encounter was recorded on my phone, which they did not take. I also had a small body camera running the entire time.

I was late to pick up my daughter from school as a direct result of the detention, which caused me and my daughter significant distress. I want to file for unlawful investigatory detention without reasonable suspicion, compelled identification in a non-stop state, and First Amendment retaliation.

fields.title: Officer stopped me while recording (gaps in story) — no location
fields.story_text: I was standing outside on a public sidewalk recording with my phone when a police officer came over and told me to stop. I said I had the right to record in public. He said I was making people uncomfortable and that I needed to leave. I told him I wasn't doing anything wrong. He then grabbed my phone and deleted my video. I was really upset. He eventually let me go but kept my memory card. I want to file a complaint because what he did was wrong and I lost my footage. I had been planning to post the video online. The whole thing took about twenty minutes and I was shaken up afterward.

fields.title: Detained outside government building (gaps in story) — no officer names or badges
fields.story_text: On May 3, 2024, around noon, I was recording outside the federal building on Main Street in downtown Nashville, Tennessee. Some officers came out and told me I had to leave. I asked why and they said it was a security area. I said I was on the public sidewalk. They told me I was being detained and made me stand against a wall for about half an hour. They took my phone and looked through it without my permission. Then they gave it back and said I could go. No charges were filed. I was embarrassed and stressed out. I want to hold them accountable for what they did to me.

fields.title: Recording at city hall — no date, no damages described (gaps in story)
fields.story_text: I went to city hall to record a public meeting. Officer James Cole, badge 3301, of the Portland Police Bureau told me I had to put my camera away. I said public meetings can be recorded under Oregon law. He said the city had its own rules. I kept recording. He grabbed my arm and walked me out of the building. Another officer, Officer Sarah Kim, badge 3344, helped him escort me out. They took my camera at the door and gave it back about an hour later. The footage was still on it. I want to file a complaint for First Amendment retaliation and being physically removed from a public meeting without legal basis.

fields.title: Vague encounter with police — most info missing (gaps in story)
fields.story_text: A cop stopped me and took my phone. I was just standing there minding my business. He said I wasn't allowed to be there. I don't remember exactly when this happened, maybe a few months ago. He was rude and wouldn't give me his name. I think there was another officer there too but I'm not sure. They kept my phone for a while. I want to sue them for what they did. It wasn't right.
